newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Kenwood damps bid talk, shares slip.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kenwood damps bid talk, shares slip.

text.p: Shares in Britain's Kenwood Appliances Plc, struggling to restore profits from its European businesses, fell on Tuesday after the company dampened bid speculation and revealed profits down by more than half.
Kenwood, which is facing moves by rebel shareholders aimed at selling the company, reported first-half pre-tax profits fell to 3.3 million pounds ($5.56 million) from 7.4 million.
By 1045 GMT the shares were down 9p at 224-1/2p, compared with their Monday close of 233-1/2p.
The company noted a report in the Financial Times that an interest had been expressed by Pifco Holdings Plc, but said no formal offer had been received.

The manufacturer and distributor of household appliances, which last year expanded with the acquisition of two Italian firms and into air conditioning, had received no direct approach from rivals, managing director Tim Beech told Reuters.

The FT had said that Pifco, a smaller household appliances firm than Kenwood, was seeking to acquire Kenwood and quoted Pifco chairman Michael Webber as saying that there was "sound commercial and industrial logic for putting the two together."
Beech told Reuters that the only approach made had been an indirect one through a non-executive director and he cast doubt on Pifco's ability to contribute to Kenwood's performance.
Kenwood remains in conflict with rebel shareholders, spearheaded by activists Brian Myerson and Julian Treger, and their UK Active Value (UKAV) group.

On December 16 Kenwood faces an extraordinary general meeting called by UKAV which has tabled a resolution that the directors be required to hold discussions with third parties aimed at soliciting a bid for the company.

In the meantime, the firm's results for the six months to October 4 did little to rebuild investor confidence. The fall in pre-tax profits came despite a ten million pound rise in turnover to 97.63 million pounds. The company kept its dividend unchanged at 3.25 pence.
Beech said the results were primarily damaged by a phase of serious market weakness and one-off factors and that its market share remained strong and its new product launches on track.
While he understood that he faced pressure from the rebels as the senior member of the management team that has supervised the trading performance, he defended his tactics.

"Some of the guns have been focused in on me. Clearly, the actions being taken are very sensible and clearly they are exactly the same actions that would have been taken by anybody else," Beech said, in reference to a profit improvement plan.
"I don't control the consumers in Italy and France (where demand for small appliances has plunged), or the weather, which was the main issue for our air conditioning," he added.

As well as seeking manufacturing efficiencies, the company's programme of profit restoration would also centre on hopes for a large number of new products coming in later this year, the results of which should start feeding in next year, he said.
The cost implications of these moves had already been charged to overheads, he added.
